title: Why he speaks of rebirth
hookLine: the Buddha tells where the dead were reborn to inspire, not to boast

cards: At a memorial, someone stands up and tells a story about the person who died. Not their résumé. A small thing.
How she always left the last piece of cake for someone else. How he answered every call from his brother, even at 3am. And people in the room quietly decide to be a bit more like that.

In the sixty-eighth sutta, at a grove called Naḷakapāna, the Buddha explains why he talks about monks and nuns and lay followers who have died, and where they went. It turns out to be the same reason.

teach.b: He starts by asking a group of young men who had left home together, Anuruddha among them, whether they're happy in the holy life. They say yes. Then he raises a fair question.
When a disciple dies, the Buddha sometimes tells people where that person was reborn, or that they reached final freedom. Isn't that a little like boasting? He answers directly.

teach.h: NOT TO BOAST, NOT FOR FAME.
teach.b: He doesn't do it to deceive people, or to flatter them, or for gain, honor or fame, or so people will think, what a teacher. He does it for people of faith who will hear it and be inspired.
A monk hears that a certain elder has died, and that the Buddha said he reached freedom. And he thinks: I saw that elder myself, or I've heard of him.
His conduct was like this, his calm was like this, his understanding was like this. And the monk turns his own mind toward that.

The sutta repeats it for nuns, for laymen and for laywomen: each hears of someone like themselves who went before, and directs their mind to the same goodness. The sutta doesn't explain here how rebirth works.
It explains the purpose of telling. A life well lived, spoken of honestly after it ends, becomes a path someone else can see. The story isn't for the dead.
It's for the ones still walking.

how: Buddhist communities remember teachers and relatives who have died at memorial ceremonies and anniversaries, where people may recall their virtues, offer food to monks, and dedicate merit to them.

o: a ceremony held to honor the dead
faith, trust, confidence in the path

games.q: why he tells it: tap the pairs.
p: the grove where this was taught
among the young men asked if they're happy
people of faith, to be inspired

s: the Buddha says he reports rebirths to show his powers
he says it's not for gain, honor or fame, but to inspire people of faith.
the sutta includes nuns and lay followers as well as monks
each hears of someone like themselves who went before.
the sutta settles exactly how rebirth works
it explains why he speaks of it, not the mechanics.

games.q: a monk hears that an elder he knew has died, and that the Buddha said he reached freedom. what does the sutta say the monk does?
o: recalls how the elder lived, and turns his mind toward that
games.why: he remembers the elder's conduct, calm and understanding, and directs his own mind toward them. that's the whole purpose of telling.

practice: Call to mind someone who has died whose way of living you admired, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, and picture one concrete thing they did: the way they spoke, or gave, or listened. Let yourself be glad they lived.
Then, like the monk in the sutta, turn your mind toward that one quality.

wordCard.voice: Saddha. Not to boast, not for fame, but so those still on the path can hear of someone who went before and be inspired.

orig.note: Pali saddhā: faith, trust, confidence. the Buddha speaks of rebirth for people of saddhā.

carryVoice: Your line: to inspire. Not to boast, not for fame, but so the living can turn toward goodness. See you tomorrow.
